generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, exams are built to support your learning, not just to grade it. A short test of anatomy or research methods checks that core ideas are secure. A written exam on a training principle asks you to weigh evidence and argue a case. Subjects treat exams differently, from lab-based science to coaching judgement and participation policy, but in each one preparing deepens your understanding and gives tutors a fair, shared view of the cohort.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport and exercise science students talk after getting back a module result that included an exam on exercise physiology.

Tom sees the exam as a hurdle now behind him. He reread his lecture notes the night before, sat the exam, and has not thought about it since. For Tom, the exam was something to survive, and its only meaning is the mark.

Amara treats the exam as part of learning. Preparing, she noticed which energy systems and testing methods she could not yet explain and went back to them, so revision taught her something. Sitting the exam to time also showed her she can reason about physiology data under pressure. For Amara, the mark is real, but so is what the exam built.

Both sat the same exam. Only Amara saw it as a learning tool, and took from it more than a grade.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, an exam is a learning tool, not just a hurdle. It supports your development, gives your tutor a level view of the cohort, and builds skills such as reasoning under time pressure. You can now explain what sport exams are for and recognise a student who treats one as something to learn from. The next lesson looks at the forms these exams take.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that showed she saw the exam as a learning tool?

items.text: She used revision to find and fix gaps in her understanding, and valued the skills the exam built.
She reread her lecture notes the night before.
She forgot about the exam as soon as it was over.
She cared only about the mark at the end.

feedback.correct: That's right. Using revision to learn, and valuing the skills built, is seeing the exam as a learning tool.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara did beyond chasing the mark.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara treated the exam as a learning tool: revision found and fixed gaps, and the exam built her reasoning under pressure. The other options only survive or chase the mark.
